🚨 PREDICTIVE PROGRAMMING? THE EXECUTION NARRATIVE CONTINUES…

Last week, I published a post documenting what I believe may be a pattern of predictive programming surrounding executions in America.

My theory was that a series of developments could be gradually conditioning the public to accept execution methods and practices that have largely disappeared from American life.

And look at what’s happened in just FIVE DAYS.

OCTOBER 5: President Trump approves the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by military firing squad. It would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.

OCTOBER 7–8: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announces that the execution is scheduled for DECEMBER 3 AT 1:00 PM, at Fort Hood—the location and approximate time of Hasan’s 2009 attack.

Then comes the extraordinary announcement:

THE EXECUTION WILL BE LIVESTREAMED FOR THE AMERICAN PUBLIC TO WATCH.

Think about that.

We have gone from discussing alternative methods of execution to discussing whether Americans should actually watch a person being executed.

OCTOBER 8–10: The announcement ignites a national debate. Political commentators, journalists, legal experts, religious leaders and elected officials are now discussing the morality, legality and appropriateness of broadcasting executions.

Even Vice President JD Vance expresses reservations about watching such a broadcast.

OCTOBER 9–10: President Trump is questioned directly about the livestream. He initially indicates approval, then says he will make the final decision, suggesting that publicly showing the execution might deter future attackers.

And simultaneously, another extraordinary development…

CHRISTA PIKE.

Remember the botched Tennessee execution that helped launch this national conversation?

Her attorneys reveal that she was on life support and believed unlikely to survive. Then, remarkably, she regains consciousness.

Today, October 10, she’s reportedly been discharged from the hospital and returned to prison, keeping the failed execution and questions about lethal injection in the headlines.

NOW LOOK AT THE PROGRESSION:

2020 — Federal regulations expand permissible execution methods.

April 2026 — DOJ moves to include firing squads in federal execution protocols.

September 30 — A botched lethal injection becomes national news.

October 5 — Trump approves a military firing-squad execution.

October 8 — The Pentagon announces plans to livestream it.

October 9–10 — A national debate erupts over public executions, with the President discussing their potential deterrent effect.

THIS IS THE VERY CONVERSATION I WAS TALKING ABOUT LAST WEEK.

My theory remains that repeated public exposure to these subjects could gradually change how Americans perceive executions, particularly military executions and methods rarely seen in modern American history.

And now the conversation has progressed beyond the death penalty itself.

We’re debating whether executions should become PUBLIC EVENTS.

The shift in what the country is discussing is undeniable.

Five days ago, we were talking about the return of military firing squads.

Today, we’re talking about Americans watching one live.

Whether this is predictive programming or simply a remarkable convergence of events, the narrative is evolving in real time.

And I believe we need to keep watching what happens next.
